flawed_step: The step claiming that partitions are balanced enough to give O(log n) recursion depth, and hence O(n log n) comparisons on every input, cannot be justified. With the first element as pivot, a sorted (sub)array's pivot is its minimum. Every partition then leaves an empty left part and a right part of size m-1, so the recursion depth is n and the work is quadratic. The idea that 'no swaps means cheap' is also wrong, because cost is measured in comparisons.
counterexample: Take the family A_n = [1,2,...,n]. At the top level, pivot 1 is compared with the other n-1 elements, all of which are greater; the left part is empty and the right part is [2..n], still sorted. The recursion repeats this, so the total is (n-1)+(n-2)+...+1 = n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which is Theta(n^2) and not O(n log n). Check for n=4 with [1,2,3,4]: pivot 1 costs 3 comparisons, then [2,3,4] costs 2, then [3,4] costs 1, for a total of 6 = 4*3/2.
assessment_summary: Deterministic first-element-pivot Lomuto quicksort has a quadratic worst case. Already-sorted arrays trigger it, using n(n-1)/2 comparisons. So the claim is false on both counts: it is not O(n log n) on every input, and sorted input is not a cheap case.
